newsitem.title: UK: Explosion rocks Belfast, injuries reported.
newsitem.headline: Explosion rocks Belfast, injuries reported.

text.p: An explosion believed to be caused by a car bomb shook central Belfast on Saturday and police said first reports indicated several people had been injured.
"I was in my office and I heard a bang and I looked out of the window and saw a car in flames," an eyewitness, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.
Police said the explosion happened in south-central Belfast near the university and city hospital. Ambulance sirens could be heard wailing towards the scene.
Few other details were immediately available.

The explosion occurred during a tense weekend in Northern Ireland after British Prime Minister Tony Blair was sternly critical of the Irish Republican Army murder last Monday of two Northern Ireland policemen.

He said the killings were staged at the very moment that Britain was exploring ways to bring the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein into Belfast peace talks from which it is excluded because of continuing IRA violence.
Gerry Adams, president of Sinn Fein, on Saturday rejected Blair's criticism of the IRA murder as "short-termism".
"No good will ever come of the current efforts to blame Sinn Fein for recent killings. Short-termism has never worked in the past. Peace-making is a difficult business," Adams said.

He was responding to Blair's remarks on his way to the G-7 summit in Denver in which he voiced outrage at the IRA's double killing last Monday which was staged after Britain lifted a ban on contact with Sinn Fein to discuss its entry into peace talks.

Adams, in a statement issued in Belfast, said Blair's government, elected on May 1, had to remove what he called "obstacles created by the last government" to its entry to the year-old Belfast negotiations.

The Sinn Fein leader, whose party and the IRA seek to end British rule of Northern Ireland, said the main stumbling block was so-called "decommissioning" -- the surrender of IRA arms, demanded by Britain.

"To do this absolute clarity is required. Especially on the issue of decommissioning. Decommissioning has not yet been removed as an obstacle in the negotiations. This remains the biggest stumbling block," Adams said.

Blair is expected to throw some light on the issue in a major speech on Northern Ireland this week after consulting his Irish partners in a three-year attempt to find a negotiated settlement to the conflict, which has killed 3,200.

The two governments lifted a ban on official contacts with Sinn Fein to hold exploratory talks on its demand to be included in the negotiations but reimposed the sanction after the two killings by IRA hit-men last Monday.

Ray Burke, who is tipped to be Irish foreign affairs minister when a new government is announced in Dublin next week, told the BBC in Belfast his Fianna Fail party was shocked by the fact the murders happened during talks with Sinn Fein.
"The doors were open to them here in Dublin as well. So I find it incomprehensible that they would go and commit this heinous crime," Burke said.

The IRA ended a 17-month ceasefire in February last year after it failed to be admitted to the negotiations because of demands that the Irish Republican Army (IRA) show willingness to give up its arsenals to prove a commitment to democracy.
Blair said on Friday that Sinn Fein had to persuade the IRA to make a clean break to its 28-year war to reunite the British province with the Irish republic and join the talks.
